title: Czekaj! · Proszę czekać.
note: CLOSED CHUNK SET — NOT A RULE. The Polish imperative is built off the perfective stem with real irregularity, and aspect has only just been named in a2_aspect. So this unit teaches five whole words to recognise and say, on exactly the terms miałem/chciałem were taught: no formation, no stem talk, nothing to take apart. FIVE FORMS: czekaj, słuchaj, idź, chodź, daj. Base-verb check against POOL: słuchać/słucham LIVE, iść/idę LIVE, chodzić/chodzę LIVE — so słuchaj, idź, chodź all sit next to a verb Dad already produces. czekać is NOT in POOL and is taught here as a new lemma, because Proszę czekać is the flagship of the polite lane and needs it. daj is opaque: dać is not in POOL, is not taught, and is never shown — daj is a single word with no relatives on screen. patrz was DROPPED: patrzeć is not in POOL either, and unlike czekać it earns no second job in the unit, so it would have been a bare orphan. weź (in the tree-node draft note) was dropped for the same reason plus a worse stem. SECOND LANE — proszę + infinitive. Framed as the safe version Dad can always fall back on, the same escape-hatch move a2_ordering_func made with Co jest dobre?. The anchor is that he ALREADY says Proszę iść prosto (POOL: proszę iść, proszę iść prosto, from a2_directions_func) — so the pattern is half-owned before it is named. Infinitives used: czekać (new), słuchać, mówić, powtarzać, all imperfective and all in POOL except czekać. FENCE — WHAT THIS UNIT NEVER DOES. (1) It never states how an imperative is formed: no 3sg stem, no drop-the-ending, no -j. (2) It never contrasts daj or idź with an infinitive — dać and iść do not appear on the same slide, in the same table, or in the same quiz item as their imperatives. The one register table pairs only czekaj/czekać and słuchaj/słuchać, and slide 4's Proszę iść prosto row is deliberately a whole phrase Dad already owns, sitting three slides away from idź and never beside it. (3) NO negative imperatives — nie rób takes the imperfective and reverses the aspect rule Dad just met; the whole nie + imperative family is absent, including from distractors. (4) NO plural or formal imperative — no niech pan, no niech pani, no czekajcie. Politeness to a stranger is handled entirely by proszę + infinitive. (5) NO 1pl — no chodźmy, idźmy. REGISTER IS THE REAL CONTENT. Because there is no morphology to teach, the unit's actual teaching load is when to use which: the short word to family and friends, proszę + infinitive to anyone, and Poproszę (already owned) at any counter where money changes hands. Daj kawę at your own kitchen table vs Poproszę kawę in a café is quiz item 5 and is the single most useful discrimination in the pack. DIRECTION IS THE OTHER HALF: idź sends the person away from you, chodź brings them towards you. English blurs this ("come to the shop with me" / "go to the shop"), Polish does not, and it is a meaning contrast rather than a form contrast, so it is safe. LEMMA CHECKS: problem, pytanie, lekarz, klucz, tutaj, prosto, po polsku, płacę kartą, herbatę, kawy (negated genitive), do sklepu, do parku, w szpitalu all verified in POOL. Jest późno was DROPPED from use item 3 — the impersonal jest + adverb frame is weather_chunk territory and Idź do sklepu. Nie mam kawy. does the same job with negation, which is properly taught.

intro.title: Five words that get things done
intro.body:
So far every Polish sentence you have built describes something: this is a table, I live in the city, mum was buying bread. Sometimes you do not want to describe anything at all. You want the other person to do something — wait, listen, come here.

Polish has one short word for each of those, and this unit gives you five of them.

Learn them exactly as they stand. They go in whole, the same way miałem and chciałem went in: single words to recognise and to say. There is nothing inside them to take apart, and you will not be asked to make any more of them. Five is enough — they are the five you will actually hear, and you will hear all of them in your first week in Poland.
intro.body_pl: Pięć gotowych słów: Czekaj! Słuchaj! Idź! Chodź! Daj!

rows: someone is about to walk off without you
before you say something that matters
you want the person to move away from you
you want the person to move towards you

intro.title: Idź and chodź point in opposite directions
intro.body:
These two are the pair worth getting right, and the difference is not politeness — it is direction.

Idź sends the other person away from where you are standing.
Idź do domu. Idź do sklepu. Idź do parku.

Chodź brings the other person towards where you are, or takes them along with you.
Chodź tutaj. Chodź do parku. — said by someone who is going there too.

English hides this. "Go to the shop" and "come to the shop with me" use the same verb shape, and English lets you say "I'm coming" when you are in fact going. Polish keeps the two apart, so ask yourself one question before you open your mouth: am I at the far end of this journey, or the near end? The word then picks itself.
intro.body_pl: Idź = ode mnie. Chodź = do mnie.

rows: you are staying, they are leaving
you are going too — come along

examples.en: Go home. Mum is at home.
examples.pl: Idź do domu. Mama jest w domu.

intro.title: Daj — and the one room where you must not use it
intro.body:
Daj takes an object, and the object behaves exactly as it does after mam. Masculine and neuter words change nothing: Daj klucz. Daj menu. Feminine words in -a swap to -ę: Daj kawę. Daj książkę. Nothing new — it is the same accusative you have been making since a1_miec.

Now the part that matters more than the grammar.

Daj is what you say to family and to close friends. It is warm at a kitchen table and rude at a shop counter. Anywhere you are paying — a shop, a café, a restaurant, a ticket window — the word is Poproszę, and you already own it.

At home, to your brother: Daj kawę.
In a café, to a waiter: Poproszę kawę.

Same coffee, different room. If you are ever unsure which room you are in, say Poproszę.
intro.body_pl: Daj = w domu. Poproszę = w sklepie, w kawiarni, w restauracji.

rows: your wife, your son, a friend

examples.en: Give me the key. I'm going home.
Give me a coffee. I'm tired.

intro.title: Proszę + the dictionary verb — the version that always works
intro.title_pl: Proszę czekać. Proszę słuchać. Proszę mówić.
intro.body:
You have been saying Proszę iść prosto since the directions unit. That whole phrase is a pattern, and the pattern is worth having on its own, because it is the safest thing in this pack.

Put Proszę in front of the plain dictionary form of a verb — the -ć form, the one you would look up — and you have a polite instruction that works with absolutely anybody: a stranger, a doctor, a receptionist, a room full of people.

Proszę czekać. — Please wait.
Proszę słuchać. — Please listen.
Proszę mówić po polsku. — Please speak Polish.
Proszę powtarzać. — Please repeat.

This is your fallback. It costs you nothing new, it is never rude to anyone, and if the short word will not come to you in the moment, this version will do the job every time. Say it slowly and you will always be understood.

rows: a stranger who has switched to English
when you did not catch it

examples.en: Please wait. The doctor is at the hospital.
examples.pl: Proszę czekać. Lekarz jest w szpitalu.

examples.en: Please listen. I have a question.

intro.title: Which one, when
intro.body:
There is no rule to remember here, only a room to notice. Three levels, and you already have two of them.

The short word — Czekaj! Słuchaj! Chodź! — is for people you are close to. Your wife, your son, a friend, a grandchild.

Proszę + the dictionary verb is for everyone else. It is the one to reach for when you do not know the person, or when there is more than one of them, or when you simply cannot remember which short word you wanted.

Poproszę is for counters. Shops, cafés, restaurants, ticket windows — anywhere money is involved.

When in doubt, go up a level. Nobody has ever been offended by Proszę czekać.
intro.body_pl: Blisko: Czekaj! Obcy: Proszę czekać. Przy kasie: Poproszę.

rows: you are at a café till

examples.pl: Czekaj tutaj. Tata jest w domu.

quiz.prompt: Your son is about to walk off and you want him to stay put. You say:
quiz.explain: Czekaj holds the person where they are. Chodź would call him over to you, and Idź would send him away — the opposite of what you want.

quiz.prompt: You are at a ticket window and the clerk must give you a moment. You say:
quiz.explain: Czekaj is for people you are close to. To a stranger behind a counter, Proszę + the dictionary verb is the version that is never rude.

quiz.prompt: You want your grandson to come over to where you are sitting. You say:
quiz.explain: Chodź brings the person towards you. Czekaj tutaj would only mean stay where you are — it does not move him at all.

quiz.prompt: You want your son to leave the house and go to the shop. You say:
quiz.explain: Chodź do sklepu is real Polish, but it means come to the shop with me — it only works if you are going too. You are staying at home, so it is Idź.

quiz.prompt: You are in a café and you want to buy a coffee. You say:
quiz.explain: All four are real Polish, but only Poproszę actually orders. Daj kawę is what you say to your brother at home — at a counter it lands as rude.

quiz.prompt: You are at your own kitchen table and your brother has the key. You say:
quiz.explain: Daj is warm with family. Poproszę klucz is not wrong Polish, but at your own table it sounds like you are buying it from him.

quiz.prompt: Which one can you say to absolutely anybody, including a stranger?
quiz.explain: The short words are all close-range. Anything starting with Proszę is safe at any distance.

quiz.prompt: The doctor said something and you did not catch it. You say:
quiz.explain: Powtarzać is the verb you already met in powtarzam. Put Proszę in front of the dictionary form and it becomes a polite request.

quiz.prompt: You are on the phone with your daughter and want her attention before you say something. You start with:
quiz.explain: Polish uses Słuchaj at the front of a sentence exactly as English uses "Listen," — with your own daughter the short form is the natural one.
The room decides. Money changing hands means Poproszę every time.

quiz.prompt: Which word sends the other person AWAY from you?
quiz.explain: Idź points away from where you are standing. Chodź points towards it. This is the pair Polish keeps apart and English does not.

quiz.prompt: Which word brings the other person TOWARDS you?
quiz.explain: Chodź tutaj is the one you call across a room. Idź tutaj is not something a Pole would say.

type_items.explain: One whole word, said as it stands. Use it with family and friends.
The same word Poles drop in at the front of a sentence, like English "Listen, …".
Idź always points away from where you are standing.
Chodź always points towards you — or along with you.
Warm with family, rude at a counter. At a counter the word is Poproszę.
Your fallback. Nobody has ever taken offence at this one, whoever they are.
Słuchać is the dictionary form behind słucham, which you already say.
Worth having ready before you need it — it is the phrase that keeps a conversation alive when you lose the thread.
Proszę is followed by the plain dictionary form — mówić, never mówię or mów. Po polsku never changes.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap (James 2026-08-06). Composed: the Proszę + dictionary-verb pattern with po polsku bolted on. Blank is the unit's teaching point — the infinitive after Proszę. Items 5-7 already type Proszę czekać / słuchać / powtarzać whole, so the pattern is still produced in full three times.
